lessons.title: What a Demerger Is and Why Conglomerates Split Up

children.text: In 2008, a Bajaj Auto shareholder owned a motorcycle maker that also happened to run an insurance and consumer finance business. After that year's demerger, the same shareholder held three separate listed companies: Bajaj Auto for two-wheelers, Bajaj Finserv for financial services, and Bajaj Holdings and Investment for the group's investments. The businesses did not change overnight. What changed was that investors could now see, value and own each one separately. Over the next decade, the financial services arm grew into one of the most valuable companies on the NSE. Chapters 1 to 3 were about companies coming together. This chapter is about why so many Indian companies are now doing the opposite.

body.text: A demerger does not create a single new rupee of cash flow. It changes who can see, value, fund and manage each business. It creates value only when the separated businesses are worth more apart, through better focus, better capital allocation and fairer market valuations, than the costs and lost synergies of splitting.

markDefs.definition: The parent company that transfers a business out in a demerger. It continues to exist and remains listed.
A business unit or division capable of operating on its own, with its own assets, liabilities, employees and contracts, that moves as a whole in a demerger.

body.text: Only a demerger puts the separated business directly into your demat account. With a hive-off, subsidiary IPO or slump sale, the value stays with the parent, and you benefit only if management uses that value or cash well. When a company announces it is "unlocking value" in a business, check which of these methods it is using.

children.text: Why Conglomerates Split: The Sum of the Parts
In Lesson 1.3 you met the conglomerate discount. To measure it, investors use a
: value each business separately at the multiples its listed peers trade at, add them up, subtract net debt and compare the result with the company's market capitalisation.

markDefs.definition: SOTP. A valuation that values each segment of a diversified company separately, usually using peer multiples, and adds the values together to estimate what the whole company would be worth if each part were priced on its own.

body.caption: Each segment's EBITDA is multiplied by the EV/EBITDA multiple of comparable listed companies in that segment.

cells: Packaged foods
Hotels

body.title: Where Sahyadri's enterprise value comes from (₹ crore)
SOTP value per share
body.prompt: Sahyadri's SOTP equity value is ₹32,000 crore and it has 100 crore shares. What is its SOTP value per share, in rupees?

body.title: Measure the conglomerate discount
body.prompt: Sahyadri trades at ₹256 against an SOTP value of ₹320 per share. What is the conglomerate discount, as a percentage of SOTP value?
body.explanation: (₹320 minus ₹256) ÷ ₹320 × 100 = ₹64 ÷ ₹320 × 100 = 20%. The market values Sahyadri at 20% less than its three businesses would be worth if each traded like its peers. This gap is the case management makes for a demerger.

body.text: SOTP values are only as good as the peer multiples chosen. Packaged foods companies in India often trade at rich multiples, so assigning 30x to Sahyadri's foods business assumes it is as strong as the best-known listed brands. If a fairer multiple is 22x, the foods segment is worth ₹17,600 crore, SOTP value drops to ₹256 per share, and the entire "discount" vanishes. Always question the multiples before believing a demerger will unlock anything.

body.title: Identify the main motive
body.question: A fictional listed group, Narmada Engineering, runs a steady, dividend-paying power transmission business and a young, loss-making EV charging business that needs large capital each year. Long-standing shareholders complain that the EV unit absorbs cash that used to be paid out as dividends, while growth investors avoid the stock because the EV story is buried inside a slow business. Which motive best explains a demerger here?
options: Regulatory separation of a lending business
Capital allocation and different investor bases
Removing a holding company discount through a merger
body.explanation: The core problem is that one business is funding another by default, and the two businesses appeal to different investors. A demerger lets the transmission company pay dividends to income investors while the EV company raises its own capital from growth investors, each at a valuation suited to its profile.

body.title: What a demerger can unlock vs what it can cost

columns.label: Potential benefits
points: Valuation closer to sum of the parts
Focused management and incentives tied to one business
Each company raises capital on its own merits
Freedom to pursue partnerships, fundraising or sales

columns.label: Potential costs
points: Duplicate boards, CFOs, auditors, listing and compliance costs
Lost shared procurement, distribution or brand benefits
Contracts between the two companies become related party transactions
A weaker company may be left with more debt
Forced selling by index funds if a new company does not qualify for the parent's index

children.text: Standalone costs add up. If the new Sahyadri Hotels needs ₹40 crore a year of additional corporate costs for its own board, leadership team, audit and listing, and hotel companies trade at 20 times EBITDA, that alone removes ₹40 crore × 20 = ₹800 crore of value, about ₹8 per Sahyadri share. The demerger has to recover that before it unlocks anything.

body.title: Name the method
body.textWithBlank: Valuing each business of a conglomerate separately at its peers' multiples and adding them up is called a sum-of-the-___ valuation.
body.explanation: A sum-of-the-parts, or SOTP, valuation is the standard way analysts and managements estimate how much value a demerger might unlock.

body.title: Why demergers are usually tax-neutral, and why the conditions matter

children.text: Receiving shares of a resulting company is not treated as income or a sale for shareholders, and the transfer of the business is not a taxable sale for the parent, as long as the demerger meets the conditions in the Income-tax Act. Broadly, all assets and liabilities of the undertaking must move together at book value, and the resulting company must issue shares to the parent's shareholders in proportion to their holdings, among other requirements.

This is one reason most Indian separations use the demerger route rather than a slump sale followed by a distribution of cash, which could be taxed at both the company and shareholder level. Lesson 4.3 shows how your original cost is split between the two holdings, and Lesson 5.1 covers the tax rules in full.

body.title: The demerger announcement rally
body.scenario: Sahyadri Industries announces it will demerge its hotels and its wires and cables businesses into two new listed companies. Shareholders will receive 1 share of each new company for every 1 Sahyadri share. The stock jumps from ₹256 to ₹290 in two days. The investor presentation shows a sum-of-the-parts value of ₹320 per share and says the demerger will be completed "in 12 to 15 months".
body.prompt: You already own Sahyadri. Do you hold, add or sell into the rally? What would you look at?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Remaining gap: at ₹290, the stock trades about 9% below the ₹320 SOTP value (₹30 ÷ ₹320). Much of the discount has already closed on the announcement alone.
2. Test the SOTP multiples: is 30x fair for the foods business? If 22x is more realistic, SOTP falls to ₹256 per share ((₹17,600 + ₹4,000 + ₹6,000 minus ₹2,000 crore) ÷ 100 crore), exactly where the stock traded before the announcement and well below ₹290.
3. Debt allocation: which company carries the ₹2,000 crore of net debt? A new company born with heavy debt could struggle.
4. Standalone costs: ask how much extra corporate cost each new company will carry.
5. Management: who will run each company? Strong, focused leadership is where real value comes from.
6. Timing and risk: 12 to 15 months of approvals, during which markets and the business can change.
7. After listing: small new companies may be excluded from indices the parent belongs to, which can cause forced selling in the first weeks.
8. A reasonable approach: holding is fine if you like the businesses. Adding after a 13% rally needs a strong view that the SOTP multiples are realistic.

steps: Confirm it is a true demerger where you receive shares, not a hive-off or slump sale
Note the entitlement ratio for each resulting company

Consider whether you want to own each business on its own, not just the combined story

cards.definition: The transfer of a business undertaking into a resulting company, whose shares are issued to the parent's shareholders in proportion to their holding.
A business unit capable of running on its own, with its assets, liabilities, employees and contracts.
Moving a business into a subsidiary the parent continues to own. Shareholders receive nothing directly.
Selling a business as a going concern for a lump sum, without assigning values to individual assets.
Valuing each segment separately at peer multiples and adding them up, less net debt.
The gap between a diversified company's market value and its sum-of-the-parts value.
Costs and lost benefits from splitting a business, such as duplicate corporate costs and loss of shared purchasing or distribution.

points: A demerger moves a business into a separate company and gives parent shareholders its shares directly. Hive-offs, subsidiary IPOs and slump sales keep the value inside the parent.
The case for most demergers is the conglomerate discount, measured by comparing market value with a sum-of-the-parts valuation.
In the Sahyadri example, SOTP value of ₹320 per share against a price of ₹256 implies a 20% discount, but using 22x instead of 30x for the foods business wipes it out entirely.
Companies demerge for valuation, focus, capital allocation, investor fit, regulatory separation and family or deal reasons.
Demergers carry real costs: duplicate overheads, lost synergies, related party dealings, debt allocation and index-related selling.
Indian examples span two decades, from Reliance in 2005 to 2006 and Bajaj Auto in 2008 to ITC Hotels and the Tata Motors split in 2025.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, tax or legal advice. Sahyadri Industries and Narmada Engineering are fictional, and their multiples are illustrative. Details of real demergers are from public disclosures and news reports and are summarised. Mentioning a company is not a recommendation to buy or sell its shares.
